headline: Sumaira Abdulali: Mumbai's improved post-Diwali AQI does not mean the air is safe; watch PM2.5
dek: The environmental campaigner said Mumbai's lower post-Diwali AQI masks the risk from fine particles, and urged people to follow PM2.5 readings rather than the headline index.
body:
Sumaira Abdulali, who describes her work on X as covering noise, sand, environment litigation, advocacy, education and awareness, wrote that Mumbai's air "looks better on paper this Diwali".

She said Mumbai's AQI on the second day after Diwali was 172, compared with 211 at the same point last year. In her view, sea winds "did most of the cleaning". She added that AQI is an average, and that averages can hide what does the damage.

Abdulali wrote that, as she told Lokmat, PM2.5 is the number to watch. She said these particles are small enough to get past the body's defences, settle deep in the lungs and enter the bloodstream. According to her post, a "moderate" AQI can still be a dangerous day for anyone with asthma, lung disease or a heart condition.

She concluded that a better score does not mean the air is safe, and tagged the Brihanmumbai Municipal Corporation's handle (@mybmc), @mpcb and Lokmat in the post.
key_quote: A better score doesn't mean the air is safe.
